title: Gum paste hydrangea
subtitle: a wired sugar flower built from small four-petalled florets assembled into a cluster
excerpt: A gum paste hydrangea is a cluster of small four-petalled florets, each shaped from gum paste, cupped to hold their form, and wired so they can be arranged on a cake. The florets are made one at a time, dried separately, then bound together with floral tape to form the finished head. The finished flowers are firm, lightweight, and can be made days in advance.
sourceNotes: Gum paste sugar flowers developed in British and Australian sugarcraft from the 1950s onward, codified in sugarcraft manuals and British City and Guilds programmes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A pliable sugar paste containing gum tragacanth or CMC (carboxymethyl cellulose) that dries very hard. Used for modelled sugar flowers and decorations that need to hold fine detail.

content.text: A gum paste hydrangea is a sugar flower built from small florets, each with four petals, assembled into a domed cluster. Each floret is cut from thinly rolled
, pressed into a cup shape, dried on a curved surface, then wired for placement. The finished cluster looks most natural in two or three related colours with a light dusting of petal dust once dry.
Allow two full days for this project: one day for making and drying the florets, one day for assembly and colouring.
Colour the gum paste in three or four shades of lilac, blue, or cream. Keep each colour wrapped in cling film to prevent drying out.
Roll a small piece of gum paste very thinly on a lightly greased board. Cut out four-petalled flower shapes using a tiny blossom or hydrangea cutter, about 2 cm across.

Hold a floret in your palm and gently press the centre with the round end of a piping tip or a ball tool. This cups the petals upward. Transfer to crumpled foil or a shaped mould to dry in this curved position.
For wired florets, push a short length of 28-gauge floral wire through the centre of the wet floret from underneath. Pinch the paste around the wire base to secure. Dry completely, at least 12 hours.
Make 20 to 30 florets per cluster. Once dry, dust lightly with petal dust from the outer edge toward the centre.

Gather the wires into a cluster and bind them together with green floral tape, starting just below the florets and continuing down the full length of the stem. The finished cluster sits on the cake or in a floral pick.

attrs.avoid: Avoid gum paste that is too dry or cold; it cracks rather than bends.
attrs.fix: Knead the paste until warm and pliable. If it cracks at the edges, knead in a tiny amount of white vegetable fat.

attrs.problem: Wire pulling free of the floret once dry
attrs.avoid: Avoid wiring a floret that is already beginning to dry; the bond will be weak.
attrs.fix: Wire immediately after shaping while the paste is still soft. Pinch firmly around the wire base with your fingertips.
